text:
*Interview with Félix Monnier, in the dining room. Second interview of the night.*

MATTHEY: Sit down, Monsieur Monnier. You are the nephew of the late master.

FÉLIX: Nephew, heir, and the only man at that table who owes money to half the people in it. You may write that down, Inspector. I would rather you had it from me.

MATTHEY: I will write what you tell me. Let us begin at dinner. When the temple bell struck nine, what happened?

FÉLIX: My uncle had us all show our watches, as he does every year. Mine showed twenty minutes to nine. He took it out of my hand, turned it over and told the whole table what was wrong with it. He made a scene of it in front of everyone. Odile did not look up. The doctor laughed, and Girard said something rude about the movement.

MATTHEY: How did that make you feel?

FÉLIX: Like a schoolboy. It is my father's watch, Inspector. He died in 1889, and it has never kept proper time since the day he gave it to me. My uncle knew that. He knew it and he enjoyed it. I made a joke, the way I do, and everyone was relieved, and then I went up to the library with my brandy and I stayed there alone.

MATTHEY: Did you ever let your uncle touch the watch?

FÉLIX: Never. He asked more than once, very kindly, for a man who had never been kind to me. I would sooner it kept bad time than went under his loupe. Ask anyone in the family.

MATTHEY: Tell me what you heard while you were in the library.

FÉLIX: At eighteen minutes past ten by my watch I heard a thump on the floor right above me, in the atelier. Then my uncle's repeater. I know that sound better than my own name. Ten slow deep notes. I counted those. Then some doubled notes, and then quick high ones, which I did not count. I was not counting anything by then.

MATTHEY: Take your time. What did you hear after that?

FÉLIX: At a quarter past ten by my watch someone went quickly up the stairs past the library door. I did not see who. The door was shut. At twenty-one minutes past ten by my watch someone came quickly down. I did not see that either. I only heard the feet.

MATTHEY: Were you frightened?

FÉLIX: Frightened? Inspector, the library is directly under the atelier. I was alone in it with brandy in me and a pocket full of other men's paper. Do you know what that looks like? A debtor under the room where the old man lay down? I have been thinking of nothing else.

MATTHEY: Who came to see you?

FÉLIX: Bastien Girard came in at thirty-two minutes past ten by my watch. We sat together there until the temple struck eleven. He wanted the rights to the repeater, and he and my uncle quarrelled about the price at dinner. Girard is not a gentle man, but he is not a fool, and he knows what he owes and what he is owed. I owe him money. Some of it. A good deal of it.

MATTHEY: How much would you say?

FÉLIX: More than I can pay, and less than Girard would like me to think. You will hear the figure from him soon enough.

MATTHEY: Did your uncle know about your debts?

FÉLIX: He knew everything about everyone. He never asked me directly. He would have, in time, and he would have enjoyed that too.

MATTHEY: Is there anything else you wish to tell me?

FÉLIX: Only this. I loved him, whatever the table thinks. He was a hard old man, and I was a fool at his table, and I am a fool now for sitting here making jokes. Forgive me, Inspector. It is what I do when I am afraid.
